triggers.text: The great door. Ninety years of paint and nobody has ever seen it open.
The Rib. The mast came down before you were born and took the cut with it. Somebody is in there: the scrape of a bar on steel, a woman laughing.
You walk up past the stand. You look back once, at the black frame of the post-house and the door in the rock, and then you don't.
The door is the colour of the rock and as old. Nobody in Knock has ever seen it move. Beside it, the hatch and the Grille, the only two mouths it has.
The toll road. North to Shale in a day, if your water holds. Nobody from Knock walks it without a reason.

barks: Hatch day. Wool for water, same as my mother did.
MOTHER says thank you. MOTHER always says thank you.
Get your goats off the apron, Afua!
I put my ear to the door. It hums.
Linnet says she's going to the city.
Race you to the tank!

triggers.text: Shale. Mud-brick and scrap around two pumps, a saloon, a flag that was a sheet once. Twenty-odd houses and a lot of empty ones.
Shale. Mud-brick and scrap around two pumps, a saloon, a flag that was a sheet once. Twenty-odd houses and a lot of empty ones.
The pumps run in short bursts, then stop, then run — on a clock nobody in Shale set.

barks: Race you to the pumps!
Mam says the Dogs eat kids.
Did you see the kite?
Mags waters it. Everyone knows.
One more and then home.

triggers.text: The dead highway lies across the sky on its piers, and under it, in the shade, the Rust Dogs have made a town out of what the highway dropped.
Shale's water, in a tank with Shale's name still stencilled on it.

barks: Looking or buying?
Posted prices.
Race you to the well!
Mam says don't.
Did you see the kite?

triggers.text: Tollhouse 9. A wall of poured concrete across the old highway, a tower with a lamp, and a gate with two sets of sandbags. Everything east of here is somebody's.
Tollhouse 9, from the inside. The wall looks the same from both sides, which is the point.
The highway runs on east. The guard at the far posts looks for a stamp you do not have.
The outriders' yard: two bikes with the guild's half-moon on the tank, a rifle scabbard on one, and the smell of fuel nobody else in the Sallow can buy.
A cage of chain-link inside the warehouse, with a cot in it and a chalk tally on the wall: days, and a sum going down very slowly.

barks: Guild water's dear.
Waiting on the caravan.
Don't look at the cage.

triggers.text: Signal Hill. A mast on the skyline with a red light that still blinks, slow as a pulse, and a track that goes up to it in switchbacks cut by somebody who meant them to last.
The top of Signal Hill. The Sallow lies under you like a map of itself: the highway, the salt pans, a line of dead windpumps to the south-east, and far west a grey smear that is Shale.
Dry Wells. Three wells with nothing in them, a water tower with something in it, and a pump station that was built to outlast the town and has.
The pump hall. Two pumps the size of houses, hammering on and off on a clock nobody in this building set, and a line going north under the floor to Shale.
The control room: a console, a pressure panel, and a chair that has not been sat in since the Burn. Something green is still lit.

The windpump graveyard. Six towers in a line across the pan, vanes locked, pumping nothing, and under them stone troughs with the dark stain of water that is not there any more. Something small bolts from the nearest trough as you come up.

The troughs are dry, but the sand around them is written over with tracks: hare, something with hooves, something with claws that walks on two toes. Game still comes here out of habit, at dawn and dusk.
Cart ruts, many and deep, going east off the pan toward a long low hill. Horse dung, not old. Something with a lot of wheels camps that way.

barks: Copper's long gone. Bearings, maybe.
Don't climb that one. It leans.
Wind's free. Parts aren't.

triggers.text: The pan. White to the edge of the world, and in the middle of it, where nothing should be, a truck on its side with its load spilled, and a dark scar in the crust behind it half a mile long. Nothing moves. The glare makes your eyes water.
A ring pressed into the crust, forty feet across, the salt fused glassy at the rim. Something heavy sat here. In the middle of it, something smaller still does.

barks: Salt's the one thing out here that keeps.
Cut while it's cool.
Mind your eyes. The glare takes them.

triggers.text: The burnt orchard. Rows of black trees the Burn left standing, and among them a dozen with leaves on, which is a thing you have not seen in your life: green, in rows, with people kneeling at their feet.

barks: Mam says the horses first.
Race you to the water wagon!
Are you from a town? What's a town like?

triggers.text: Ninebridge. The old highway walks out over a gorge on nine concrete legs and a town has grown on its back: tents and stalls and welded boxes the whole length of the deck, lamps on poles, a hum of people buying. The ninth span is missing. Below, a river that has not run in ninety years.
Ninebridge, from the east: the road runs down to a gorge and a bridge with a town on it, and the first thing on this bank is a metal platform with a cage.
The deck ends in air. The ninth span lies in the riverbed in three pieces, with a market stall still bolted to one of them. The way across is four planks along the south parapet.
The auction block: a welded platform, a counter, and a cage with a cot in it. A chalk board lists today's lots by number and sum. The sums are people.
The porters' camp under the west ramp: tents, a fire, and forty people who carry the bridge's goods on their backs when the guild says carry — sitting down, today, with their straps off.

barks: Paper's up again.
Twelve for the crossing, and they call it a bridge.
Don't buy futures from a man who smiles.
The ninth span? Fell the year the river stopped.
Straps off. Straps stay off.
They forecast we lose. Let them carry it, then.
Three days, they said. We can sit three days.
Lot four's young. That'll go high.
I came for a cook. They've only got debtors.
Fen hates it. He's good at it, though.
Mind the planks.
Guild deck. Guild rules.

of_shrine_sign.name: The sign of the open sky

triggers.text: Openfield. Rows and rows of green in the glass, which is a thing you have seen once before in your life, on a smaller scale, north of Shale; two long timber halls; a well with a wheel on it; and people in grey scarves bending to the soil who straighten as you come, and look at the sky, and go back to it.
Openfield, from the east: a burial ground of cairns under a dead windpump, and past it the green rows the Choir has coaxed out of the glass.
The fields. Every third row is grey: leaves curled and spotted, stalks gone soft at the root, the smell of something sweet going wrong. The rows between are green and do not know yet.
The burial ground: cairns in rows under the open sky, no names on them, a dead windpump turning for nobody. One grave is new.

barks: Every third row. We pull it and it comes back.
The sky keeps no books.
Don't drink from the north trough; the Elder says.
Sing or don't. The soil doesn't mind.
Are you from the bridge? Did you see the planks?
Petra says don't talk to strangers. You're a stranger.
I can sing the whole sky-song. All of it.
They feed us first. First! Nobody ever fed us first.
Came from the Sump. Don't go to the Sump.

triggers.text: The Sump. A concrete bowl sunk in the glass where the city's storm drains once came up for air, pumped dry by hand and picked over by two camps that do not speak: scrap cabins on the west rim, tents on the east, and between them, at the bowl's north end, a tunnel mouth with sandbags across it and a lamp burning in daylight.
The bowl: wrecks, drums, a crane-arm somebody has been trying to raise for a year, and a machine on its side with its legs folded, the city's kind, dead so long the scavengers use it as a bench.

barks: Grel says the tunnel's ours. The Tanners say otherwise. The guild says keep digging.
Scrip on the fourth day. Always the fourth day.
Don't cross the bowl after dark.
Hesk says the tunnel's ours. Grel says otherwise. The guild pays both, which should tell you something.
There's a door down there that never opened.
West rim's got the better cabins. We've got the better knives.

triggers.text: The tunnel comes up through a hole the Sump cut in a pump-room floor. Pumps like Cistern 9's. A supply pipe like Cistern 9's, cut through, dry. The lamp the scavengers hung still burns. Everything else has been dark for forty years, and smells of it.
A line on the corridor wall at shoulder height, brown, where water stood for a season after the pumps stopped and then went down and did not come back.
The dormitory. The cots are made. Some of them are not empty, and have not been for forty years, and lie the way people lie who decided to.
The great-door hall. Sandbags against the inside of the door, and crates, and a table, and then — the marks are still on the floor — the sandbags dragged away again, and the door still shut.

exits.label: The stair down to the Sink
The avenue east, to Old Market
The lane north, to the Spire close
The gate road north along the Wall, to the Ring
The river road south along the Wall, to the Docks

triggers.text: Meridian. Towers first, miles off, grey against grey; then the Wall, poured concrete five storeys high, running out of sight both ways; then, when the road reaches it, a gate the size of a door, a booth, a lamp, and a line of people who have been waiting since before you came over the last rise.

The Precinct. Swept asphalt, lamps that all work, a tram rail, buildings with numbers on them, and people walking as if they had somewhere to be by a time. Nobody looks at you. A camera on the lamp-post does.
A square between the tenements with a standpipe, a bell on a post, and a notice board under glass. Everything that happens here has been posted first.
The Loop's Precinct platform: a raised deck, a shelter, a tram on the rail with its doors open and nobody in it, and a board of district names with a fare beside each.

barks: Curfew's at nine. The bell's never late.
Mind the camera; it minds you.
Water's rationed since the Sallow business. Point eight.
The schedule holds.
Papers.
Keep to the avenue after dark.
Third day in the line. They say the hearing's Tuesday.
The Ring's burning again. They don't care.
My face isn't on their machine. That's the whole problem.

exits.label: The avenue west, to the Precinct
The stair down to the Sink
The east street, to Lantern Row

triggers.text: Old Market. The avenue gives out at a dead mall with its roof gone and a thousand people inside it, and the streets round it are stalls, and the stalls are everything: noodles, cells, cartridges, cloth, paper, chrome in boxes, a tram that still runs and a kiosk that still talks. Nobody here walks as if they had somewhere to be by a time.

The mall's central court under the open sky: a dead escalator, a metal deck worn bright, pink and blue light from tubes somebody salvaged, and a container with a hatch in it and a board beside the hatch, which is where everyone in Meridian who needs something done ends up looking.

The standpipe square. The dial is turned down and the queue is forty long and getting louder, and the two wardens at the square's edge have the look of men counting. Somebody at the front says the Precinct drinks what the market doesn't.
The east street runs on toward Lantern Row under strings of dead bulbs and a warden who says WORKS before you ask.

barks: Half-Price pays half. That's the name.
Don't buy chrome from a box you can't open.
The kiosk said my name. It said my dead name.
The Precinct drinks what we don't.
Wardens count the market twice a day and never like the answer.
Point eight. For us it's point six.
The dial's theirs. The thirst's ours.
Auntie Wen's. Two Tolls, a bowl. Three, with meat; don't ask which.
Best gossip in Meridian is in this queue.

exits.label: The stair up to the Precinct
The stair up to Old Market

triggers.text: The Sink. The stair comes down out of the Precinct's lamplight into a dark that drips, and the dark is a city: the old streets under the elevated road, flooded to the knee, flooded to the roof, lit by work-lamps on cables and by nothing. Boardwalks on stilts go out across the water to where people live. Something is pumping, far off, slowly, like a heart that has been told to.

The Sink, by the market stair: a concrete shelf, a kettle, a wall of names, and below it the dark water of the under-city with its boardwalks going out across it on stilts. Something is pumping, far off, slowly.

The first pier of the stilt-walk has lines chalked up its side, one above the other, each with a year. The top line is above your head. Somebody has chalked next spring's already, a hand higher, with a question mark.
The pump house: the one building in the Sink with the Precinct's white lamps on it, and two wardens at its door who are not here to keep the Sink dry. Through the wall, the slow thud of the pumps.
The clinic: a brick shell with a sodium lamp over the door and a queue that has learned to sit. The only light in the Sink that is the colour of a kitchen.
Three people with no chrome and skin the colour of the water stand up from a fire as you come along the walk. Nobody says anything. It is the kind of nobody that means turn round.

barks: Line's a hand higher this year.
Pumps run for the Precinct. We run for the stairs.
Ocho's free. Ocho's always free. Don't ask what it costs him.
Don't go east on the walk. The Pale don't like faces.
Sit. The queue sits.
Teng buys. Teng buys anything that was ever warm.
Spring's coming up the stair this year, you watch.
Mind the third board.
Water's warm. That's the worst of it.

exits.label: The street west, to Old Market

triggers.text: Lantern Row. The street comes out of Old Market's dead bulbs into live ones: salvaged tubes in every colour that still lights, strung over a canal that throws them back. Music from three doors at once, none of it the same song. A bridge, a boat, a queue outside something pink. Somebody is shouting odds.
The Loop's Lantern Row stop: a metal deck with a tram on it and the Row going away south under its tubes, pink and cyan and gold, over the black line of the canal. Somebody is shouting odds.

The pit: a sunk metal floor inside a chain fence, four white lamps, bleachers of crates, and a card on a post with tonight's names. The crowd stands three deep. The floor has been washed and it shows.
The Lantern: a container with a violet tube over the door and a smell of warm electronics. Reveries by the hour. The sign says MEMORIES — YOURS OR BETTER.
The street runs on east under dead tubes toward Bridgeward, and a chain across it with a sign: WORKS. Two Gilt lean on the chain and do not say works.

barks: Anvil's three to one. He's always three to one.
The Velvet's a queue tonight. Try the hall.
Don't buy a reverie you can't put down.
Gilt pay in Crown coin. Don't take it; it's counted.
Somebody's stranger on the card again.
Twenty on the small one.
He went down in the second last week. Took the dive, you watch.
Mab pays. Mab always pays. That's why Mab's rich.
Boat's two. Bridge is free and further.
Canal's warm. Don't ask.

triggers.text: The Stacks. Two megablocks a street apart and forty floors high, grey, each window a different light, each balcony a different washing. The street between them is a canyon with a tram at the bottom of it. Somewhere above you a thousand doors are shutting for the night.

Block Seven's lobby: a concrete hall the height of three floors with a market in it, a board of floor notices, a committee office with a door, and a stairwell in a cage. The lifts are dead; there is a panel beside them that says so in the Plan's own words.

barks: Nine's dry again. Twelve's pumping.
Forty floors and the lift says *as per schedule*.
Committee meets in the lobby. Everyone shouts; Gudrun writes.
Don't rent above twenty. The water doesn't.
Fitch has water. Fitch always has water; ask him whose.
The board says Nine, Twelve and the roof. The board always says that.
Stairs. Nine floors. I count them every night.

exits.label: Down: nine floors to the lobby

triggers.text: Floor nine. A corridor of doors round a dead core, lit by lamps on cables that somebody keeps lit; washing on lines between the lamps; the smell of a hundred stoves. Every door has a number and most have a name chalked under it. 9-14 has neither.

barks: Nine's dry. Twelve's pumping. Same every night.
Gudrun says the committee's meeting. Gudrun's been saying.
Ulla hears the lifts. Ulla hears everything that's stopped.
9-14's been empty since the Ostrows went to the Ring.

triggers.text: The roof of Block Seven, forty floors up: the whole of Meridian under you in its haze, the Spire a grey needle to the south, the Wall a line, the Sallow beyond it going to nothing. Up here the air moves. A tank on a pad in the middle; beds of real dirt to the west with things growing in them; a deck of trays to the east under an awning, greener, humming. Two groups of people who are not looking at each other.

barks: Beds are dry by noon. Tank's full by six. Do the sum.
Twelve pumps at two. I hear it through the floor.
Mama Deel grew tomatoes up here the year I was born.
Trays don't need dirt. Trays need the tank.
Latch comes Thursdays. Don't talk to Latch.
Best view in Meridian and nobody comes up for it.
You can see the Sink from here if you know where it isn't.

exits.label: The chain west, to Lantern Row

triggers.text: Bridgeward. The chain behind you, and ahead a street of chop-shops and salvage heaps running to a bridge that goes out over nothing and stops. Three kinds of paint on the walls, each over the other. A red light blinks on a mast. Somebody at the bridgehead is charging money to stand on it.
The Loop's Bridgeward stop, a metal deck over a street of salvage with a broken bridge at the end of it and a red light blinking on a mast. Three kinds of paint on every wall.

The bridgehead: a chain across the deck, a booth, two Rustmouths with shotguns and a slate of prices, and beyond them the bridge going out over the dry river to where it isn't any more. A notice on the booth in Crown print.

The Saints' tower: a dead relay mast with a red lamp on it that somebody keeps lit, and under it a brick shell full of radios that do not work, arranged like an altar, and people sitting with them, listening.
The deck ends in torn rebar and air. Forty feet down, the dry river; across it, the far bank and the Docks' cranes, close enough to hear and no way to reach.

barks: Toll's five to stand on a bridge that goes nowhere.
Three paints on the wall. Mine's under all of them.
The girl at the tower said my name yesterday. I've never met her.
Rustmouths take for the Crown. Gilt take for the Gilt. Pale take what you've got two of.
The Dogs had the garage. Then the Rustmouths had the bridge. Then the Dogs had the Sallow.
Haul's weighed Fridays.
Boss says the Crown pays by the car. The Crown doesn't know what a car is.
Listen. There — under the hiss.
She says true things. That's the trouble with her.

triggers.text: The Crown's lift lobby. The car that costs nothing opens on tile that has been washed, a lens on a post with a green light under it, and two wardens whose grey is clean. Through the gate, light: real light, through glass, on leaves. Nobody here is in a hurry, which is the first thing money buys.

The terraces. Domes of old glass over a promenade of planters that are green all the way through, a pool that reflects a sky it does not have to share, and a hall at the end with its doors open on music. The air has no taste at all. People in clothes that have never been mended look at you the way the lens did, and decide, and go on.
Through the gate over three wardens. Somewhere a bell has started that is not for dinner, and the people on the promenade are going indoors the way birds go off a field.

decision.text: You went into the Crown over its wardens.

news.text: somebody went up to the Crown over the lift wardens during the Masque

triggers.text: The Masque. A hall under the biggest dome, lit like noon at night, strings somewhere, and a hundred people in the Crown's season showing their faces to one another and to the lens over the door, which is the point of a Masque up here: everyone is seen. At the far end a lectern with the Committee's crest, and nobody at it yet.

A studio: a chair in good light, a machine that hums, and the walls hung with portraits of people who look like the people on the promenade but better, older, finished. Under each a date that has not happened yet.
House Ashby-Crane's salon: older money than the hall, quieter, a crest over the door with a crane on it, and a girl at the window who is not looking at the view.
The kitchens: heat, steam, forty people in white moving fast, and a lift that goes down to Old Market with the day's rubbish and the night's help. Nobody up here has ever seen this room.

The parapet. Under it, all of Meridian in haze: the Precinct a grid, Old Market a stain, the canal a thread, the Stacks a wall, the broken bridge a finger pointing at the Docks. You cannot see the Sink at all. That is the point of up here.

barks: Vane's season. Everyone says so, so it must be.
The near end. Have you heard? The near end of a bridge.
The Concern sent a man. The Concern never sends a man.
I don't go down. Fenwick goes down. Look what it did to him.
The Chair, tonight. They say the file already knows.
Honora won't duel. Honora buys.
Smile. The lens likes a smile.
Forty covers. Forty! For people who don't eat.
Down by the lift at four, or walk.
Don't look at them. They don't look at you.
Green all the way through. It's the water. They have the water.
Mind the beds.

exits.label: The lane south, to the Precinct

triggers.text: The Spire close. A square of clean paving behind the Precinct, lamps that work, and at its north end the Archive Spire going up into the haze until you lose it: the city's records, ninety-odd floors of them, its doors shut behind scaffolding. The Crown's glass catches the light on its shoulders. Broad steps run up to the doors, and the steps are familiar the way a word on the tip of your tongue is familiar.

The Court of Accounts. A long hall with a bench at the far end, a rail across the middle, benches for the public, and on the bench a grey unit with a brass plate and two ledgers, very still. Behind it, against the wall, a second chair, dark wood, with dust on the seat. Nobody sits in the public benches who does not have to.

The catalogue: shelves of bound indexes to the ceiling, reading tables with green-shaded lamps, a terminal, a counter with a keeper behind it, and in the far corner a stair going up into the dark with a lens on a post at its foot and a porter at a desk beside it.
A room behind the court that smells of ink and a stove. Shelves of bound copies, a desk with a lamp, a cot made with corners. Somebody lives here, and has for a long time.

barks: The steps reopen R49. It says so on the board.
Don't stand on the scaffold. They count the planks.
My sister had a case. Eleven times called. Then they stopped calling.
Ninety-one floors. Nobody's been to the top that came down to say.
Case four hundred and something. They said today.
It reads everything. Bring everything.
Nobody speaks for you unless you bring them.
Slip first. Then the index. Then wait.
Ninety-one landings. I've been to the fortieth.
R30 works. On schedule.
Every stone numbered. Every stone back where it was.
Papers.
The steps are closed. The works say so.

exits.label: Down: ninety-one landings to the catalogue

triggers.text: Landing ninety-one. The stair comes up into a corridor with no sound in it at all: drawers of steel to the ceiling on one side, a dark room humming on the other, and at the end a round door with a brass plate. The air is cold and dry and tastes of nothing. Something up here knows you have arrived; there is no lens to say so, and you know it anyway.
A gallery along the west wall with a stone sill at waist height and nothing past it but haze and, very far down, the city.

barks: Slip.
Nobody reads up here. We dust.

exits.label: The gate road south, along the Wall to the Precinct

triggers.text: The Ring. North along the Wall the road runs between the Wall's grey face on one side and, on the other, towers with nothing in them, a salvage yard, smoke, and somewhere ahead the sound of engines. Nobody here has a card. Nobody here is counted, except by each other.

Clover: the Loop's last halt, a metal deck outside the Wall where the rail comes out of a portal and stops against a buffer. A turnstile and a lens on the portal. Below the deck, a ring of cracked asphalt round a field of broken pillars, and the smell of alcohol fuel.

Clover: the old cloverleaf's ramps cut down to a ring of asphalt behind low piers, with tyres stacked at the bends and a gantry at the start line. Tyre marks everywhere, black over black. Through the middle, where a ramp fell, a straight line of rubble somebody has been driving across.

Leven: the lower floors of a tower called Eleven before the Burn, squatted all the way up to where the floors stop. Washing on wires across the windows. A door with chalk on it, and a woman inside counting something.
A salvage yard: girders on trestles, steel cut into lengths and stacked by weight, a torch going, and a board of tallies with tower numbers on it. Twelve people working and none of them talking.

A dead tower's shell, open to the sky, rubble to the knee. Something in the back of it, under a fall of concrete, that is not rubble: legs folded under it like a dog asleep, and a sensor head the size of a bucket. It does not move. Children's handprints in chalk on its flank.

barks: Bello. Bello. Always Bello.
Two on the Mule to finish. Nobody bets the Mule to win.
Dorota's flag. Nobody jumps Dorota's flag twice.
The Crown came down last season to watch. They clapped like it was a play.
Somebody always goes into the tyres at the cloverleaf.
Ninety-one on the count. Ninety-two since Tuesday.
Rain tank's at a hand. Ha-eun says a hand lasts.
They don't burn a tower with a count. That's what the count's for.
Nobody inside the Wall has ever counted us.
Steel's weighed at the gate.
Tower Six came down sweet. Forty ton.
Ruben pays. That's all I know about Ruben.
The Wall doesn't look at you out here. That's the good of it.
The line's at the gate. The Ring's for when you stop queueing.
Emil says the Mule has one more season in her. Emil says that every season.
Alcohol, two jugs. The Heron drinks three.

triggers.text: Two-Twelve: the Line's last halt, a platform of plate steel under the Teeth with the rails running out into nothing beyond it. Above, the town climbs the mountain in steps of tin and timber all the way up to a wall of rock, and over the rock, faint even by day, a green glow. Somebody has painted on the platform's edge, in letters a yard high: NO LAMPS DOWN.

The Line board over the platform, which has said ARRIVALS — NONE since you stepped off, flickers. The letters run, stop, and run again: DESIGNATE. YOU'RE LIT UP LIKE THE GARDENS. LODGE, AFTER DARK. — K. Then: ARRIVALS — NONE. Nobody else on the platform looks up.

Number Six: a headframe of riveted girders over a cage house, a winding engine gone cold, and a lamp room with every lamp on its rack. People sit along the spoil heaps in their work clothes, not working. Two of the Concern's security stand at the cage in clean grey with nothing on their boots. Nobody in the Skirts calls them anything but the Clean.
The Lodge: a ski lodge from before the Burn, its beams black with ninety winters of stove smoke, long tables, and a board of names. It smells of wet wool and soup. Whoever is here is the Shift.

Footgate. A fence, a gate, the Clean, and behind them the valley station where the funicular goes up into the rock on a track as steep as a ladder. The car sits at the bottom with its doors shut. A board on the station says, in clean print, SERVICE SUSPENDED — INDUSTRIAL ACTION. Somebody has chalked under it: NO LAMPS DOWN, NO CAR UP.

The Weighhouse: a long concrete shed that weighed ore before the Burn, with the scale's iron deck still set in its floor by the door. A queue on a bench inside. A woman in clinic white writes on a board. Nobody in the queue is talking.
Cascade: the old main run, stepped with concrete and lined with stalls from the Lodge down to the Line. Everything is priced in scrip. Halfway up, a wall of notices: lost, found, for sale, gone.
The Pond: a dry reservoir where the old resort made its snow, cracked concrete with a low wall round it and wrecks piled for seats. Blood and sawdust on the floor. A slate on a post.
Nursery: shacks on the old beginners' slope, tin and pallet and the doors of pre-war cars, three rows deep, with gardens in every gap. Children, smoke, washing, a cough in every third doorway.

barks: No lamps down.
Eleven. Say the number.
The Window cut the ration again. Let it.
Maren says hold. We hold.
The Clean don't get their boots dirty. Look at them.
Scrip only. Tolls at the changer.
Turnip, two scrip. Two. It's a good turnip.
Provision's up again. Everybody's up again.
You can see the gardens from the top of Cascade, at night. Green. Like a lamp left on.
Nobody comes back from the Weighhouse. Nobody comes back from the hill. Same thing.
Mind the cough. It's catching, or it isn't. Nobody knows.
Cabbage again.
My father dug Six for thirty years. Six dug him back.
There's an orange tree up there. Kes says. Kes has seen it.
Baek. Baek. Always Baek.
No chrome in the Pond. The Pond's rule.
Two scrip on the stranger. For the colour.
The Line's late. The Line's always late.
Six to one at the booth. Six to one.
Whatever comes up the Line is for the Window.
Over the line. That's all. Over the line.
They say you go up to the gardens. Service.
My paper's heavier than I am.
Rosa's pour. Rosa's rules.
Dust's for people with something to lose. Deal me in.
Six East. Say it again and I'll drink to it again.

triggers.text: The cage stops with a jolt that goes up your spine, and the dark comes in at the gate. Cold, and the smell of wet stone and old powder. A lamp on a hook. A heading going east, and a long way off down it, nothing.

The workings open out: a room cut out of the seam, the roof held up by pillars of coal left standing in rows like the legs of a table. The rows go east into the dark, and the pillars there are thinner than the ones you passed.

Four Ways: a brick station under a clock tower, two roads of track, an island platform, and a town that keeps the station's hours. The clock is right. Everyone you can see has looked at it in the last minute, and most of them have looked at their own wrists after.
The road south runs on the bed of a railway that is not there any more: you can see where the sleepers lay, a stripe of darker earth every yard, all the way to the horizon and Tollhouse 9.
Four Ways' street: houses of timber and container steel, a watch house with a bell, and everything facing the station like chairs facing a stage.
The signal box stands on brick legs at the platform's end, glass on three sides, levers in a row like the teeth of a comb. Inside somebody is writing in a book by a lamp.

The Canopy: a market under ironwork that once held a roof, now holding tarps, lamps and washing. Water by the cup, bread by the slice, bolts by the pound. A boy goes round the stalls calling the next train like a hymn.
The old south branch: a straight half-mile of rail with a chalk line across it, two handcars on the stop-block, and a slate on a post with names and times.

barks: Water by the cup. Clean cup, clean water.
Seven o'clock for Yard Nine and the west. Seven o'clock.
Clock says ten past. Clock's right.
Bolts by the pound. Rust is extra.
The through went by again at two. Didn't even blow for us.
Twenty-five a leg. Robbery, and they call the others robbers.
Don't step on the track. The watch counts it.
I've waited three days for a wagon to Tollhouse. The Line's faster when it runs.
Batista's pour. Watch the clock.
Gorse? Good guard. Bad luck. Kettle's bad luck.
Through-running. Means through your pocket.
Pump, don't pray.
Two Tolls on the left car.
Mind the points at the far end. They bite.
Bell's for the watch. Clock's for everybody.
My grandmother kept the down line. Before the guild had the tickets.
Out of timetable on the track and the watch shoots. Everyone knows that.

triggers.text: West Halt: a platform, a water tower, a keeper's house and a handful of others, half of them with their doors nailed. A board on the platform once said TRAINS STOP ON REQUEST. Somebody has painted THROUGH over it in guild green, and somebody else has scratched the green half off again.
The water tower's ladder has been pulled up and its hatch padlocked with a new lock. From inside, once, somebody coughs, and somebody else hushes them.

barks: The through doesn't stop. Didn't blow, even.
Length money. Ask the guild where it went.
Bread's dear this week. Everything's dear.
Flag's up if you want the seven o'clock.
Openfield's a day south. They feed you if you dig.

triggers.text: East Halt: a platform built for a town, and the town gone. Fourteen people live here now, a water tower with a cracked tank, and a row of houses with their doors nailed and the names of the people who left chalked on the boards. East, the Line goes into a cutting toward the Teeth.

barks: Forty-five of us when the stops were stops.
The through goes by at two. You can set your teeth by it.
Nobody buys water from a halt nobody stops at.

triggers.text: Yard Nine: a depot in a bowl of dead cars, three sidings of them rusting into the grass, an engine shed big enough to sleep a village, and a still house that smells of bread gone wrong. The main line runs through it all and out the other side.

In the engine shed, on the left road, an engine stands cold over its pit: long, square-nosed, armoured over the cab with plate somebody riveted on by hand. DORCAS, in paint, on the nose. On the right road, the bay where the other one stands when it is in is empty and black with oil.

barks: One engine and the through gets every path. You do the sums.
Dorcas'll go again. Ida says.
Grain from Openfield, alcohol from the still, miles from the alcohol. That's the Line.

triggers.text: Kettle Cut: the Line and the old road go through a notch in red clay banks twenty feet high, side by side, with no room for anything else. In the ditch lie two cars on their sides, opened like tins. At the far end a pre-war boiler, the kettle, rusts in the reeds.

A lamp, hooded green, coming down the rails from the west with no engine behind it: a handcar, four people pumping, and the sound of it carried a long way in the cut. It stops by the wrecks. Somebody lays a sleeper across the rails. Somebody lights a cigarette and puts it out again.

Gull Stilts: a village on legs, standing in the sea. Houses of tin and pallet and car doors on posts driven into a drowned town's streets, boardwalks for streets, boats for carts, and under the boards, a yard down in green water, the tops of street lamps. The water has a skin on it like a bruise, purple and gold where the light catches it, and the smell of the village is fish, smoke and something under both that belongs in an engine.

The Ebb Steps: the broad steps of some drowned hall going down into the water, and half the village on them. A small shape in a weighted net lies on the bottom step with the tide going out over its feet. A woman kneels by it with her hands flat on the net, not crying. Nobody speaks. A man begins to say a name and stops when she looks at him.

The Greta: a car ferry from before the Burn, run aground in the middle of the village and never refloated, her car deck open to the sky. Benches where the cars stood. At the bow end, under two lamps, a chart table with a book on it as thick as a brick, and an old woman who looks up from it as if she knew you were coming aboard.

A steel container on a pontoon, lashed to the Greta's stern, painted in the guild's colours under the rust: the tide post. SALT — TWINE — MEDICINE — FISH BOUGHT. A man in a good coat behind the counter, writing.

The Jesty: a drowned hotel's roof, the only thing in the bay taller than the stilts, with its parapet a hand above the water at high tide. Against its south edge a guild barge lies broken-backed where it struck, her hold open, divers going in and out of it like gulls at a gutted fish.

Coker's dive stage: a grate platform with a hand-cranked air pump on it, a coil of hose as thick as a wrist, ladders going down into the green, and a woman counting under her breath with her eyes on a line in the water.

barks: Mind the boards by the Greta. Rotten since the spring.
Mackerel tastes of the rig. Eat it anyway.
Slack at four. The city's table says.
Somebody fell off the Gut last week. Somebody always does.
Twine's dearer than the fish now.
Lua hasn't mended a net since. Who would.
Hold the end. No, the end.
What the water wrecks, the water gives. That's the Book.
Salt. Sacks of it. Dry, some of it.
Two of the barge crew drowned. Guild men. Still men.
Out on the ebb. Same as my mother.
You can see the lamp posts from here at low water.
Don't swim under the Gut. Not now.
Oona's got the Book open. Somebody's in trouble.
Page nine. Always page nine with her.
The guild pays the anchorage. The widows eat. Don't say it louder.
Tide boat's at six, if Mele's sober. She's always sober.
Salt up from the city again. Dearer.
Rigs folk in on the launch. Smell them before you see them.

triggers.text: Hum: a steel island on four legs, rust-red and salt-white, with a flame on a stack at its western corner that has not gone out in ninety years. Under your boots the whole platform trembles, steady as a held note. That is the turbine, burning the gas Hum lifts out of the sea floor to lift the oil. Forty people live up here on nothing that grows.

The turbine hall: the noise is a wall you walk into. Three machines the size of trucks, two dead, one alive and shaking its housing with something like contentment. Somebody has chalked on its casing, in a careful hand that has been gone over every year: DON'T LET HER STOP.

A catwalk over open water to Lean, the dead platform, which lists to the south as if it were listening to something under the sea. A lamp burns in a glass room on its derrick: the shore's light, fed by a hose of Hum's gas.

barks: Don't let her stop.
Lamp oil, rig diesel, and tar for the Stilts' hulls. That's Hum's whole catalogue.
Pressure's down again. Hamid says she's tired.
Fish again. Fish from the Stilts. They hate us and they sell us fish.
One tanker a month. One. And the guild wants two.
My grandfather climbed up a leg with a knife in his teeth. Now look at us. Accountants.

triggers.text: Down the moonpool ladder, rung by rung, out of the hum and into the cold. The leg is a steel well thirty yards across, ribbed like a throat, with the sea breathing in and out of its bottom. Your lamp finds pipes as thick as a man going down into the dark, and a stair.

The stair ends in water. Below the waterline the cold closes on your chest like a hand; the sea is in the leg to your waist and black where it is deeper. A hose of bubbles comes up from something far below and breaks under your chin with a smell of rotten eggs.

The valve chamber: a manifold of pipes going down through the floor of the leg and out along the sea bed, toward the shore. One great wheel, its spindle bright where somebody has turned it, recently, and turned it a long way.

Blackcap: the last tank of a drowned oil terminal, standing out of the bay like the cap of something buried to the eyebrows. The water round it is not water-coloured. It moves slowly, like syrup, and gives back the sky in purple and gold. The smell gets into your teeth.

The tank's roof, black and warm underfoot. A pump on the north rim that is not ninety years old: new hose, new clamps, a guild padlock, and the guild's mark stencilled on its housing. The hose goes over the rim and down into the tank.

exits.label: The river road, round by the Wall to the Precinct's gate

triggers.text: Carrick: the Docks. The river road comes off the Wall's shoulder and down onto a quay as wide as a field, and the city you just left is behind you across a river with no water in it. Cranes along the far side of everything, three storeys high, most of them dead and one of them moving. A freight shed with a train under its roof. A fenced yard lit white in the middle of the day. Boxes stacked into a town. The smell of salt, fish, diesel and bodies working.

The end of the Line: a brick freight shed as long as a street, its roof glass gone to frames, a platform down one side, a buffer stop at the far end with a lamp on it, and steam from the engine standing in the light. Beyond the shed's mouth, cranes, and a quay that smells of the sea. The guard calls it from the step: CARRICK. ALL CHANGE. NOWHERE TO CHANGE TO.

The water stairs: worn granite going down into the Basin, green to the third step, with iron rings in the wall for boats. Above them, the quay: cranes, a fenced yard lit white, a stone building with a flag, and a town of stacked boxes. The city is across a river with no water in it, close enough to hear its bells.

Under Crane Six a forty-foot box lies split on the quay where it fell in the night, one end crushed into the concrete. Beside it a tarp over something the shape of a man, with a pair of boots out from under it. Dockers walk round the tarp without looking at it, the way you walk round a hole you know is there. Nobody has moved the box. Nobody has moved him.

The Stand: a white line painted along the quay, worn to a ghost by boots, where the dockers stand at dawn for the call-on and the gang-masters walk down it choosing. A tally board on a post. Gang Nine's names on it have a chalk line through them.

The Bond: a yard fenced in good mesh with a light on every post, white light, even at noon. Sealed boxes stacked inside with the closed eye stencilled on their doors, a clean office at the back, and two guards at the gate in grey that has never been near a crane. The Concern's, by the Harbour Act: inside the fence the Harbour Master's word stops.

The river stairs go down through the wall onto the bed of a river that stopped ninety years ago. Down there, ships: real ones, long as streets, sitting on the dry bed where the water left them, rust to the rails, with washing on their rails and smoke from their funnels and ladders down their sides. Children on a gangway. Blue stakes driven in among them in a line, new.

The Customs House: stone, four storeys of it, the only building on the quay with every window glazed. CUSTOMS on the lintel in letters cut for a thousand years, and under it, painted for ninety: HARBOUR MASTER — BY THE ACT. The steps are worn hollow in the middle. A guild guard sits on them with a shotgun across his knees as if the steps were a chair he had been given.

barks: Gang Nine stood down. No tally, no funeral. That's the guild.
Six lifts heavy and Six lifts at night. Ask why.
Platt calls you or he doesn't. Don't look at him.
The Bond lights never go off. What do they need to see?
Dmytro never dropped a box. Never.
Seven o'clock's in at five. Never before.
Through comes in at the throat and the Bond takes it. Nobody gets a look.
Water for the engine, coal for nobody. Sixty drinks.
Mullet off the wall. Small, but they're here.
Grigor's steps, Grigor's fish. Ask him nice.
The tide boat's in on the flood. Salt from the delta.
Blue stakes. Somebody's building something over us.
My grandmother was born on the Star. So was I.
Cradle's five a head. Ask Kobby. Ask at night.
The river stopped and we didn't.
Espe's soup is mostly hot. That's the best thing about it.
Four to a box. Five if you're friendly.
Oksana's girl coughs all night. You get used to it. You don't.
Please stay outside the line.
Everything in the yard is under bond.
The seal is the manifest. The manifest is the seal.

triggers.text: Number Four: a headframe of old black steel over a bowl of rock and pine on the Teeth's south face, a wheel turning in a snowmelt stream, a smelter's smoke going straight up in the cold, and sixty people's washing. Nobody here wears the Concern's grey. Somebody has painted on the cage house, in letters a yard high, NO PAPER PAST THIS POINT.
The track comes up from the Line's cutting in long loops through the pines, and over your head the bucket line's cable runs the same way in a straight line, singing a little in the wind.

The col: a saddle of rubble and old snow between two shoulders of the Teeth, and a hut of split logs with its door to the south. North, below you, the Skirts lie down the far slope in their smoke, and over them the rim of Halcyon's caldera with its gardens glowing. South, the path drops through the rock to Number Four's lamps.

Two shapes on the switchback ledge where the path turns back on itself, in grey under white snow-capes, with carbines across their chests and no lamp. They are not hiding. They are waiting, the way men wait who have been told the hour.

barks: No paper past the cage.
Tin's tin. Nobody up the hill gets a say in it.
Snow on the col. Anybody coming over will be cold.
Mind the spoil. It moves.
Six cuts a day out of the pillars. Old men's pillars. They left us plenty.
Three this year. Three. Count them on the board.
She counts the tags every night. Every single one.
The cutter took my arm out. I can't lift much. I can lift my own kid.

triggers.text: The old level: a drive cut through grey rock ninety years ago, with the rails still in its floor and the water a hand deep along one wall. Somebody has chalked arrows on the props, one way to the cage, one way to daylight, one way UP — THE COL — LONG. It is very quiet, and then, a long way off, it is not: a slow, patient sound, like a very large animal turning over in its sleep.

In the stope, half out of the black water, a machine the size of a cart lies against the face with its cutting head raised: armoured, segmented, with the closed eye on its housing under the rust. A lamp on its flank, green, blinks once. Then again. The sound you heard was it, shifting its weight.

Sawtown: a street of timber houses under a hill of stumps, a sawmill the size of a church on a race of fast brown water, and out on the lake a grid of log walkways round pens full of floating trees, every one with a mark cut in its butt. It smells of resin and wet ash and frying. It has been raining since before you arrived and will be raining after you leave.

The north track ends here at a loading stage of old concrete, the rails running off south-east into the trees toward Yard Nine. Somebody keeps the last hundred yards of it oiled and bright, though the weeds own the rest.

On the walkways, sorters with pike poles walk the logs into their pens by the marks on their butts: a crow's foot to the north pens, a hook to the south. A woman at the head of the boom calls every mark aloud and a boy writes it down.

barks: Crow's foot, north pen. Hook, south.
The boom pays what the mark says.
Mind the walkway. The Water's colder than it looks.
Rain. Of course rain.
Six marks short on the tally again. Somebody's cutting.
Dorit's stew. Don't ask what it was.
Ridge and Bottoms. Two years now. You'd think it was a hundred.
Mikkel Brandvold. Nice boy. Shame.
The barge goes down at six. If the river's up.
Timber!
Watch your back-cut.
The Bottoms can keep the flats. Mud and money.

triggers.text: Ashby Dam: a wall of pre-war concrete across a valley, a road along its top, grey water to the north as far as the rain lets you see and a river in a gorge to the south. ASHBY in letters as tall as a house on the downstream face, the paint ninety years gone and the letters still there in clean stripes where the moss will not grow. At the east end a gatehouse with one lit window. Under your feet, very faintly, the dam hums.

The path up from Low Landing comes out of the gorge onto the east bank under the dam's face, where the tailrace boils white out of the turbine hall's mouth and an old woman's washing hangs on a line between two dead pines.

The inspection gallery: a concrete corridor running the length of the dam inside it, a man's height and a man's width, with a drain along its floor and the whole of Ashby Water on the other side of the left-hand wall. The wall sweats. Somewhere along it, water is running that should not be.

Low Landing: a quay of pre-war concrete a quarter of a mile long on a brown river, three barges and a hulk tied to it, a winch house with the guild's green on its door, and behind it all the grey shells of buildings so big the town looks like something that has crawled into the corner of them to keep dry. The high-water line is painted on every post at the height of your head. Nobody lives below it.
The road to the city runs south from the Landing on an embankment above the flood meadows, straight, with the river on its right hand all the way.

barks: Barge down at six. If the dam lets her.
River's low. River's always low.
The guild's winch. The guild's men on it. The guild's river, they'll say next.
Half a load and a whole fare. That's the Wet.
Heave.
Two more months on my paper. Two.
Don't talk to me. He's watching.
Above the line or not at all.
The dam'll go one spring. My gran said so. Her gran said so.
Fish? In that? Eels, maybe.
